content: Ensuring accurate HIV testing data is challenging. One effective method to address this is by using unique identifiers for individuals, which can help track retesting and prevent double reporting. This approach is particularly useful when electronic systems are available to link data through these identifiers. Another strategy involves recording prior testing information in the HIV Testing Services (HTS) client register. This allows retests to be identified, counted, and subtracted from the total number of tests performed for the same individual. Population-based surveys are also a valuable tool to avoid double-counting retests. These surveys are especially beneficial for assessing testing coverage among hard-to-reach populations. In many settings, routine program monitoring cannot collect key population-specific data, so the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends investing in surveys to estimate service use that is more representative and statistically robust. Disaggregating HTS data at the national level is critical to ensure that key populations are accessing services. Optimal analysis of HTS data requires breaking down service statistics by multiple dimensions, such as age, sex, diagnosis, service delivery point, and key population status. However, compiling these figures from paper-based registers can be time-consuming. Special efforts are needed to design paper-based tools that support data disaggregation without overburdening those responsible for data collection and analysis. Variables to consider for disaggregation include age groups (e.g., <1, 1–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–49, 50+), sex (male, female, transgender), test results (positive, negative, inconclusive, unknown), population categories (e.g., pregnant women, key populations, adolescents, TB patients), geographic area, and service delivery points (e.g., facility-based, community-based, or other settings). Monitoring and evaluation of HTS have evolved from simply measuring the number of people tested to assessing knowledge of HIV status among different populations and estimating the proportion of people living with HIV (PLHIV) who have been diagnosed. There is growing interest in identifying underserved populations and improving engagement with high-risk groups who are unaware of their HIV status. The effectiveness of HTS is now measured not by the volume of testing but by the number of people who know their HIV status, particularly those at highest risk. Prevention, care, and treatment services along the HIV cascade are essential. Some populations, such as pregnant women or TB patients, are more accessible for HIV testing, and their data are easier to capture. However, marginalized populations and young people living with HIV require more targeted efforts to measure and address their needs, especially in areas with high rates of new infections. Analyzing HIV testing data by site type is crucial for determining where national programs should allocate resources. Each program should maintain a reliable list of HTS sites, categorized by service delivery setting (e.g., antenatal care clinics, TB clinics, community-based services). High-quality HTS depends on accurate diagnosis and effective linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. Monitoring quality starts with reviewing national testing policies, test kit quality, diagnostic accuracy, and the quality of counseling and referrals. Indicators should also assess compliance with human rights norms, particularly for key populations. WHO recommends tailored strategies to increase testing uptake among priority populations. These include provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) in generalized epidemics for all individuals attending health facilities, and in concentrated epidemics for those presenting with conditions indicative of HIV. Community-based HTS with linkage to care is recommended for key populations in all epidemic settings. Testing for couples and partners, with support for mutual disclosure, is also encouraged, particularly in antenatal care settings. For pregnant women, PITC in prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs is widely implemented. However, HIV testing is only the first step in a cascade that spans over 18 months of risk if breastfeeding. Offering HTS to partners and family members of PLHIV is an efficient way to identify additional cases and support earlier linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART). In sub-Saharan Africa, many serodiscordant couples are unaware of their status, leading to new infections. Interventions for serodiscordant couples include condom provision, male circumcision, STI treatment, daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for the uninfected partner, and immediate ART initiation for the HIV-positive partner. For infants and children, WHO recommends early virologic testing of HIV-exposed infants at 4–6 weeks of age to enable timely ART initiation. For adolescents, national health systems should stratify data by adolescent-specific age groups (10–14, 15–19 years) to assess testing uptake, treatment linkage, and follow-up trends. WHO encourages countries to revise consent policies to reduce age-related barriers to HTS access. Key populations, due to their increased risk and vulnerability to HIV, are a priority for scaling up acceptable HTS and ensuring strong linkages to prevention, care, and treatment. The marginalized nature of these populations makes service provision and monitoring particularly challenging. WHO emphasizes the need for strategies that address the unique needs of key populations while ensuring human rights compliance. Finally, monitoring the proportion of PLHIV who know their status is critical, as this knowledge is the entry point to the continuum of care. Disaggregated estimates can reveal gaps in diagnosing PLHIV and should be globally reported for target populations. High coverage of early virological testing in infants supports timely ART initiation and counseling to prevent seroconversion.
